title: The Ius Commune and the Early Modern Times

slides.title: Two contemporary voices on the reception
slides.text: The lecture opens with two sources rather than a definition. Hermann Conring, 1643: since the 15th century doctors of Roman law have been consulted more frequently than before in council meetings and courts of law. And Bernhard Walther, 1552, stating the operative rule: if a custom of the land is doubtful and uncertain, judgment shall always follow the WRITTEN laws — meaning the laws taught at the university. Read together they show how the reception actually worked: not by an act of enactment, but through a rule about what to do when local custom is unclear. Doubt about custom is the doorway through which learned law enters.

cards.q: According to Bernhard Walther (1552), what happens when a custom of the land is doubtful?
cards.a: Judgment follows the written laws — that is, the learned law taught at the universities. Doubt about local custom is the doorway through which Roman law enters practice.

slides.title: The phases of the reception
slides.text: An EARLY phase: the ecclesiastical courts receive learned law as early as the late Middle Ages, the 13th to 15th centuries — unsurprisingly, since canon law already lived by Roman law subsidiarily. The PEAK comes with the secular courts at the beginning of the modern era, around 1500. The institutional trigger is the imperial reform of 1495 and the Imperial Chamber Court it created, staffed HALF with nobles and HALF with jurists. Put a court in place that is half learned lawyers, and learned law follows automatically.

cards.q: Name the two phases of the reception of learned law and the institutional trigger of the second.
cards.a: Early phase: the ecclesiastical courts, 13th–15th centuries. Peak: the secular courts around 1500. The trigger was the imperial reform of 1495 and the new Imperial Chamber Court, composed half of nobles and half of jurists.

slides.title: Imperial Chamber Court and Imperial Aulic Council
slides.text: Two supreme courts of the Empire, and the difference between them is INDEPENDENCE. The IMPERIAL CHAMBER COURT (Reichskammergericht) was composed of equal numbers of representatives of the emperor and of the Imperial Diet, which made it independent OF the emperor. Its seat was Speyer, and from 1693 to 1806 Wetzlar. The IMPERIAL AULIC COUNCIL (Reichshofrat) was an advisory body to the emperor that also performed judicial functions, and it therefore remained DEPENDENT on him; it sat at the imperial court — in Vienna from 1612 to 1740 and again 1745 to 1806. A litigant thus had a choice between a court the emperor did not control and one he did.

terms.def: Supreme court of the Empire from 1495, half imperial and half Imperial Diet representatives — hence independent of the emperor. Seat Speyer, from 1693 Wetzlar.
Advisory body to the emperor with judicial functions, remaining dependent on him. Seat at the imperial court, in Vienna 1612–1740 and 1745–1806.

cards.q: What is the decisive difference between the Imperial Chamber Court and the Imperial Aulic Council?
cards.a: Independence. The Chamber Court was staffed equally by the emperor's and the Imperial Diet's representatives, so it was independent of the emperor (Speyer, from 1693 Wetzlar). The Aulic Council was the emperor's own advisory body exercising judicial functions and stayed dependent on him (at the imperial court, Vienna 1612–1740 and 1745–1806).

slides.title: The Aulic Council's archive
slides.text: The Reichskanzleitrakt of the Vienna Hofburg housed the Imperial Aulic Chancellery and the Aulic Council until 1806, and roughly 80,000 files of the Council fill three floors of the Austrian State Archives at Minoritenplatz. It is a reminder that the Empire's judicial business was real and voluminous, not ceremonial.

slides.title: What the reception changed in the courtroom
slides.text: The most concrete slide of the lecture — court practice before and after, point by point. BEFORE: the judge must be EQUAL TO THE DEFENDANT, because this is a class society; the judge only PRESIDES and judgment is passed by the court community; proceedings are PUBLIC and ORAL, in GERMAN. AFTER: judges must have STUDIED at a university, and they always apply learned law where no conflicting local custom is proven; the judge both presides AND passes sentence; proceedings are SECRET and IN WRITING, in LATIN. Note the price: the reception brought professional judges and a rational system, and it took away publicity, orality and the vernacular. The allegory on the slide sets a praetor against a German count.

cards.q: Contrast court proceedings before and after the reception of learned law.
cards.a: Before: the judge had to be of equal status to the defendant, he only presided while the court community passed judgment, and proceedings were public, oral and in German. After: judges had to have studied at a university and applied learned law wherever no conflicting local custom was proven, the judge both presided and sentenced, and proceedings were secret, written and in Latin.

cards.q: What did the reception cost the parties in court, even as it professionalised justice?
cards.a: Publicity, orality and their own language: proceedings became secret, written and Latin, conducted by university-trained judges rather than by a community of the defendant's equals.

slides.note: Sloupce jsou ve slidu vedle sebe a v textové vrstvě se prolínají; pořadí „před / po recepci" je tady srovnané podle obsahu.

slides.title: The Lothar legend debunked
slides.text: The theoretical question: HOW did the reception come about? The old answer was the 'Lothar legend' — that Justinian's laws were reintroduced by order of Emperor Lothar. Hermann Conring demolished it in 1643: the widely held belief is 'not only uncertain, but also incorrect'. The importance of this is methodological. If Roman law had been enacted, its validity would rest on an act of a ruler. Since it was not, its validity has to be explained case by case, through practice and custom — which is exactly what Conring goes on to argue.

terms.def: The belief that Roman law was reintroduced in the Empire by an enactment of Emperor Lothar. Refuted by Hermann Conring in 1643.

cards.q: What is the Lothar legend, who refuted it and why does the refutation matter?
cards.a: The belief that Justinian's law was reintroduced by an enactment of Emperor Lothar. Hermann Conring refuted it in 1643. It matters because Roman law's validity then cannot rest on a ruler's act — it has to be shown case by case that a rule took hold in practice and custom.

slides.title: The ius commune
slides.text: The reception is a PAN-EUROPEAN phenomenon, and what it produces is a pan-European law: the IUS COMMUNE (German: gemeines Recht — the lecture asks you not to translate it into English). Its formal position is subsidiary: it applies only where domestic law does not. Its actual position is another matter — it increasingly supplants domestic law, precisely through Walther's rule about doubtful custom. There was resistance, in Tyrol and Saxony among other places. And two regions never received it at all: ENGLAND and SCANDINAVIA. That exception is the whole reason the common law becomes a separate topic in this course.

terms.def: The pan-European learned law formed by the reception of Roman and canon law (German: gemeines Recht). Formally subsidiary to domestic law, in practice increasingly displacing it.

cards.q: What is the ius commune, what is its formal rank, and what actually happened to that rank?
cards.a: The pan-European learned law produced by the reception (German: gemeines Recht). Formally it applies only subsidiarily, where domestic law does not reach — but in practice it increasingly supplanted domestic law, since doubtful local custom was decided by the written learned law.

cards.q: Where was the ius commune NOT received, and where was there resistance?
cards.a: No reception at all in England and Scandinavia. Resistance to acceptance in Tyrol and Saxony, among other places.

slides.title: Where the ius commune applied
slides.text: The map of its territorial scope — and of the two blanks, England and Scandinavia.

slides.title: Law reforms (Reformationen)
slides.text: The formula to remember: the ius commune was the CAUSE, the MEANS and the END of legislative activity in the early modern era — it provoked the reforms, supplied the concepts they were written with, and was the standard they aimed at. Municipal law reforms: Nuremberg 1479, Worms 1498, Ptuj 1513, Freiburg im Breisgau 1520. Land law reforms: Bavaria 1518, Württemberg 1555. Two Austrian cases go the other way: the Land Ordinance for Tyrol of 1526 ADHERES to domestic law, and the Austrian land law drafts of 1526–1654 never entered into force at all.

cards.q: In what triple sense was the ius commune behind early modern legislation?
cards.a: It was the cause (it provoked the reforms), the means (it supplied the concepts and the drafting) and the end (it was the standard they aimed at) of legislative activity.

cards.q: What is notable about the Austrian law reforms of the early modern era?
cards.a: They largely failed or resisted: the Land Ordinance for Tyrol of 1526 adhered to domestic law, and the Austrian land law drafts of 1526–1654 never entered into force.

slides.title: Policey ordinances and the Carolina
slides.text: A false friend first: POLICEY is not 'policy' and not the police. Policey is the precursor of modern ADMINISTRATIVE law — epidemic control, building and fire regulations, begging, prostitution and so on; the slide's plague doctors with their beak masks, and Vienna's infection-control measures from 1541, are Policey in action. Policeyordnungen often carry private-law matters as well. And 1532 brings the CONSTITUTIO CRIMINALIS CAROLINA, the procedure for judging capital crimes: it unifies and modernises criminal procedure in the Empire — but, note, it too applies ONLY SUBSIDIARILY, behind land law.

terms.def: Not 'police' and not 'policy': the early modern precursor of administrative law — epidemic control, building and fire rules, begging, prostitution. Its ordinances often contain private law too.
Criminal procedure for capital crimes in the Empire; unifying and modernising, but applying only subsidiarily behind land law.

cards.q: What does 'Policey' mean in early modern law?
cards.a: Not the police and not policy: the precursor of modern administrative law — epidemic control, building and fire regulations, begging, prostitution and the like. Policeyordnungen often also contain private-law matters.

cards.q: What is the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina, and what limits its force?
cards.a: The imperial procedure of 1532 for judging capital crimes, unifying and modernising criminal procedure in the Empire. Its limit: like the ius commune it applies only subsidiarily, behind land law.

slides.title: Mos italicus against mos gallicus
slides.text: The two ways of doing legal scholarship, and the exam likes the contrast. The MIDDLE AGES: the centre is northern Italy — the MOS ITALICUS. Its method is SCHOLASTICISM; the Corpus Iuris Civilis is treated as RATIO SCRIPTA, written reason; the gloss is binding; and differences from domestic law are treated as merely apparent, which produces the concordance literature reconciling the two. The EARLY MODERN ERA: the centre moves to France — the MOS GALLICUS. Its method is HUMANISM; the Corpus Iuris is seen as a HISTORICALLY DEVELOPED product, not timeless reason; scholars want direct access to classical Roman law, going behind the gloss; and domestic law appears as a misguided development. The shift is from a timeless authority to be harmonised into a historical text to be reconstructed.

terms.def: The Italian manner: scholastic treatment of the Corpus Iuris as ratio scripta, with the gloss binding and domestic law harmonised with it.
The French manner: humanist treatment of the Corpus Iuris as a historically developed text, seeking direct access to classical Roman law behind the gloss.
'Written reason' — the medieval view of the Corpus Iuris Civilis as authority valid by its rationality rather than by enactment.

cards.q: Contrast mos italicus and mos gallicus.
cards.a: Mos italicus (Middle Ages, northern Italy): scholastic method, the Corpus Iuris as ratio scripta, the gloss binding, differences from domestic law treated as merely apparent (concordance literature). Mos gallicus (early modern, France): humanist method, the Corpus Iuris seen as a historically developed product, direct access to classical Roman law behind the gloss, domestic law regarded as a misguided development.

cards.q: What changes in the STATUS of the Corpus Iuris between the two schools?
cards.a: It stops being timeless authority and becomes a historical document. For the mos italicus it is ratio scripta, written reason to be harmonised; for the humanist mos gallicus it is a text with a history, to be reconstructed critically — which is why the gloss loses its binding force.

slides.note: Ve slidu jsou dva sloupce vedle sebe a textová vrstva je prolnula — vyšlo z ní „středověk: humanismus". Správně je středověk = mos italicus + scholastika, raný novověk = mos gallicus + humanismus. Ověřit na obrázku slidu.

slides.title: Usus modernus pandectarum
slides.text: Conring's debunking of the Lothar legend in 1643 has a constructive consequence. If domestic law was not displaced by a single act, then for EACH INDIVIDUAL RULE one must examine whether it has gained a foothold in customary law. At the universities this produces the USUS MODERNUS PANDECTARUM — embedding domestic law inside the established learned doctrine. In legal practice the result is a mixture of domestic law and ius commune, the IUS ROMANO-GERMANICUM. Neither pure Roman nor purely domestic: a working amalgam, and the state of European private law until the codifications.

terms.def: The early modern university treatment embedding domestic law within the received learned doctrine, rule by rule, after the Lothar legend fell.
The practical mixture of domestic law and ius commune — the law actually applied before the codifications.

cards.q: What is the usus modernus pandectarum, and what follows from it in practice?
cards.a: The university treatment that embeds domestic law within the received learned doctrine, examining rule by rule whether it took hold in customary law — the consequence of Conring showing that no single act had introduced Roman law. In practice it produces a mixture of domestic law and ius commune: the ius Romano-Germanicum.

slides.title: The rise of the Habsburgs
slides.text: The accumulation, by dates: 1282 the Duchy of Austria; 1477 Burgundy, including the Netherlands; 1504/16 Castile and Aragon — that is Spain with large parts of Italy and the overseas colonies; 1526 Hungary and Bohemia, meaning today's Hungary, Czech Republic, Slovakia, large parts of Croatia and Romania and parts of Poland, Serbia and Ukraine; 1580 Portugal with its overseas colonies. Almost none of it by conquest: this is inheritance and marriage, which is why the introductory lecture's point about personal union matters — these lands are acquired one crown at a time and keep their own law.

cards.q: Give the stages of the Habsburg accumulation of lands with their dates.
cards.a: 1282 the Duchy of Austria; 1477 Burgundy with the Netherlands; 1504/16 Castile and Aragon (Spain, large parts of Italy, the overseas colonies); 1526 Hungary and Bohemia; 1580 Portugal with its colonies.

cards.q: Why does the Habsburg rise leave a patchwork of legal orders rather than one law?
cards.a: Because the lands were acquired by inheritance and marriage, one crown at a time, as personal unions. Each realm kept its own institutions and its own law; only the ruler was shared.

slides.title: Reformation and Counter-Reformation
slides.text: The confessional map of Europe: Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican, Orthodox, Muslim. It closes this topic and opens the next ones — the Westphalian order exists because that map could not be unified by force, and the Peace of Westphalia is the legal answer to it.
